title: Magnets
standard_text: Recognise that magnets attract magnetic materials and that like poles repel and unlike poles attract; a freely suspended magnet comes to rest pointing north-south. Make a magnet by the stroke method and the electrical method, and compare the strength of magnets. Recognise uses of magnets in everyday life (summary of the MOE Primary Science Syllabus).
meta_desc: Free Primary 3 science worksheets for Singapore pupils on magnets: magnetic materials, poles, attract and repel, making magnets and electromagnets, and uses of magnets. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Like poles repel; unlike poles attract.
key_sub: Magnets attract iron, steel, nickel and cobalt.
body_html:
How to think about it

A magnet attracts magnetic materials: iron, steel, nickel and cobalt.

  • Every magnet has a north pole and a south pole. The force is strongest at the poles.
  • Like poles repel. Unlike poles attract. A freely hanging magnet points north-south.
  • Make a magnet by stroking a steel object in one direction with one pole, or by the electrical method (a coil of wire round an iron nail, connected to a battery).
Example

Two magnets push apart. What can you say about the facing poles?

Push apart means repel

Like poles repel

Answer: They are the same pole (N–N or S–S).

Example

How can you make an electromagnet pick up more paper clips?

Add more coils of wire

Or use more batteries

Answer: Make more coils or use more batteries.

Common mistakes

  • Thinking all metals are magnetic. Aluminium, copper, gold and silver are not.
  • Thinking a steel object that attracts a magnet must be a magnet. Only repulsion proves it is a magnet.
  • Stroking back and forth when making a magnet. Stroke in one direction with one pole.
  • Judging a magnet's strength by its size. Test it with paper clips.

faq.q: Which materials does a magnet attract?
faq.a: Magnetic materials: iron, steel, nickel and cobalt. Aluminium, copper, plastic, wood and glass are not attracted.

faq.q: How do I make a magnet?
faq.a: Stroke a steel object many times in one direction with one pole of a magnet, or wind a coil of wire around an iron nail and connect it to a battery.

faq.q: How can I tell if an object is a magnet?
faq.a: Bring it near each pole of a known magnet. If it repels one of the poles, it is a magnet.

items.q: Can a magnet attract an object without touching it?
c: Yes. The magnetic force acts over a distance.
items.e: A paper clip jumps to a magnet before they touch.

items.q: Which of these would a magnet pick up: a nickel button, a plastic ruler, a wooden pencil or an aluminium drinks can?
items.e: Only iron, steel, nickel and cobalt are magnetic. Aluminium, copper, brass, gold and silver are metals that are not.

items.q: Will a magnet attract a steel drawing pin?
c: No, it is not attracted to a magnet.
Yes, it is attracted to a magnet.
items.e: Iron, steel, nickel and cobalt are magnetic. Most other materials, including many metals, are not.

items.q: Why are fridge doors usually made of steel on the outside?
c: Steel is magnetic, so fridge magnets stick to it.
items.e: Magnets attract iron and steel, so they can be used to sort and separate materials.

items.q: Where is the magnetic force of a bar magnet strongest?
items.e: More paper clips stick to the ends.

items.q: Two toy train carriages join with magnets. The back of the yellow carriage has a north pole. The front of the orange carriage has a north pole. Will they join?
c: Yes, they join, because unlike poles attract.
Yes, any two magnets always join.
No, they push apart, because like poles repel.
items.e: Unlike poles attract; like poles repel.

items.q: What happens when two north poles are pushed together?
items.e: Like poles repel.

items.q: What happens when a north pole and a south pole are brought together?
items.e: Unlike poles attract.

items.q: Two toy train carriages join with magnets. The back of the orange carriage has a north pole. The front of the purple carriage has a north pole. Will they join?
c: No, they push apart, because like poles repel.
Yes, they join, because unlike poles attract.

items.e: Unlike poles attract; like poles repel.

items.q: Where is a bar magnet strongest?
items.e: Paperclips cling to the ends.

items.q: The south pole of a magnet attracts one end of another magnet. Which pole is that end?
items.e: Like poles repel; unlike poles attract.

items.q: Explain what happens when these magnets are brought together.
c: Two north poles face each other, and like poles repel.
Magnets only work when they touch.
A north pole faces a south pole, and unlike poles attract.
items.e: Look at the two ends that face each other.

items.q: Three magnets are pushed together in this order. What happens between the middle magnet and the right magnet?
items.e: Look at the two ends that face each other: like poles repel, unlike poles attract.

items.q: Does a magnet have to touch a paperclip to pull it?
c: No. Magnetic force can act at a distance.
Only if the paperclip is big.
items.e: A non-contact force.

items.q: Can a magnet attract a paperclip through a sheet of paper?
c: Yes. Magnetic force passes through paper.
items.e: Try it!

items.q: A magnet is held above a sheet of paper with a steel paper clip on the other side. What happens?
c: The paper clip is still attracted through the paper.
items.e: Magnetic force can act through non-magnetic materials such as paper.

items.q: What does attract mean?
items.e: Unlike poles attract.

items.q: A magnet is held above a sheet of wood with a steel paper clip on the other side. What happens?
c: The paper clip is still attracted through the wood.
items.e: Magnetic force can act through non-magnetic materials such as wood.

items.q: Which two poles are facing each other?
c: the south pole of the left magnet and the north pole of the right magnet
the north pole of the left magnet and the north pole of the right magnet
the south pole of the left magnet and the south pole of the right magnet
the north pole of the left magnet and the south pole of the right magnet
items.e: Look at the letters on the two inside ends.

items.q: The north pole of a magnet attracts one end of another magnet. Which pole is that end?
items.e: Like poles repel; unlike poles attract.

items.q: A magnet is held above a thick steel plate with a paper clip under it. Why is the paper clip attracted less?
c: The steel plate is attracted and takes up much of the magnetic force.
The paper clip is too heavy.
items.e: Magnetic materials such as steel can block some of the magnetic force.

items.q: The north pole of one magnet is brought near the south pole of another magnet. What happens?
items.e: Like poles repel; unlike poles attract.

items.q: What is the main advantage of an electromagnet?
c: It can be switched on and off.
items.e: Cranes in scrapyards switch electromagnets off to drop the metal.

items.q: Which of these is a metal that a magnet would NOT pick up: a silver bracelet, a steel spoon, an iron bolt or iron filings?
items.e: Only iron, steel, nickel and cobalt are magnetic. Aluminium, copper, brass, gold and silver are metals that are not.

items.q: What is the electrical method of making a magnet?
c: winding a coil of wire around an iron nail and connecting it to a battery
hitting a nail with a hammer
items.e: This makes an electromagnet.

items.q: Why must you lift the magnet away at the end of each stroke?
c: so that you stroke in the same direction every time
items.e: Stroking back and forth does not make a good magnet.

items.q: Which object can be made into a magnet by stroking?
items.e: Only magnetic materials can be made into magnets.

items.q: A magnet made by stroking can lose its magnetism. Which action would make this happen?
c: dropping it many times or heating it
stroking it again in one direction
items.e: Rough handling and heat can weaken magnets.

items.e: This keeps cupboard doors closed.

items.q: Where is a magnet used like this: magnets separate steel cans from aluminium cans.
items.e: Magnets are useful in many everyday things.

items.q: Why is a compass useful when hiking in a forest?
c: Its magnetic needle points north, so you can find your direction.
items.e: The needle is a small magnet.

items.q: What keeps a fridge door shut tightly?
c: magnetic strips in the rubber seal
items.e: The magnets attract the steel body of the fridge.

items.q: Steel is mostly made from which magnetic metal?
items.e: That is why steel is magnetic.

items.q: Are all metals magnetic?
c: No. Only some, such as iron and steel.

items.q: Which metals are magnetic?

items.q: How are magnets used at recycling centres?

items.q: How are magnets used in some toys, such as fishing games?
c: Magnets on the rods attract the steel parts on the toy fish.
The fish float up by themselves.
The fish are made of plastic only.
items.e: The steel parts are attracted to the magnets.

items.q: How do magnets help to keep things neat in a toolbox?

items.e: Steel tools are attracted to the strip.

items.q: Siti wants to find out which of three magnets is the strongest. Which is the best method?
c: Look at the colour of each magnet.

items.e: A stronger magnet holds more paper clips.

items.q: How could you find which end of an unlabelled magnet is north?
c: Bring it near the north pole of a labelled magnet: the end that is repelled is north.
items.e: Use repulsion to test.

items.q: A big magnet held fewer paper clips than a small magnet. What does this show?
c: The paper clips are not magnetic.
The small magnet is not a magnet.
The size of a magnet does not always tell how strong it is.
items.e: Test the strength; do not judge by size.

items.q: A pupil moved a magnet closer and closer to a paper clip on a table. She measured the distance when the clip first moved. What is she finding out?
c: whether the clip is made of plastic
items.e: A stronger magnet attracts the clip from further away.

items.q: A magnet attracts a steel paperclip through a wooden table. What does this show?
c: Magnetic force can pass through wood, which is not magnetic.
items.e: Through non-magnetic materials.

items.q: Two ring magnets on a pencil float one above the other with a gap. Why?
c: Like poles are facing each other, so they repel.
The magnets have lost their magnetism.
Unlike poles are facing, so they attract.
items.e: Repulsion holds the top magnet up.
